The user is happy to batch **multiple loosely-related issues into one PR** to keep review cadence
flowing. Stated 2026-08-08 during wave 8.

**Why:** CodeRabbit gives one review per hour org-wide, so a wave of N single-issue PRs costs at
least N hours of review chain whatever order it runs in. The file-ownership graph caps how much can
run in *parallel*; the review slot caps how fast anything *lands*. Batching cuts the number of
cycles, and it is the only lever that moves the real bottleneck. See
[[project-v2-hot-file-contention-caps-parallelism]] for the other half of the constraint.

**How to apply:**

- Batch by **shared file surface first, topical relation second**. Two issues that both touch
  `facade.rs` belong together whether or not they are conceptually related, because splitting them
  guarantees a rebase. Two issues in the same subsystem that interact semantically (one changes
  where auth state comes from, the other what happens when restore fails) belong together because
  splitting them makes the second rework the first.
- 2–3 issues per PR is the working size. Do not build one giant PR: review quality drops, and
  CodeRabbit has a [[project-coderabbit-150-file-cap]].
- Give each issue its own commit inside the batch, and a `Closes #N` line per issue in the body.
- When adding scope to an agent already mid-build, tell it to finish the original issue coherently
  first and add the second on top — and to ship the first alone if the second turns out much larger
  than scoped. A blocked bug fix is worse than an extra review cycle.
- Still hold a batch behind a genuine blocker. Batching changes how work is grouped, never whether
  a dependency edge is respected.

Related: [[feedback-closes-vs-part-of-issue-hygiene]] (one `Closes` per finished issue),
[[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]] (the orchestrator owns slot timing).

**Reaffirmed and strengthened 2026-08-19 (wave 11):** "I would like each of the PRs to close more
than one issue (if possible and appropriate)." Treat a single-issue PR as needing justification,
not as a default. This applies to slices already planned but **not yet opened** — re-batch them
mid-wave rather than waiting for the next wave.

Two things make re-batching easier than it looks mid-wave:

- A hot-file slot **frees the moment its PR merges**. The "one PR per wave per hot file" rule is
  about PRs in flight together, not the wave as a calendar unit. Once the `facade.rs` claimant
  merges, a later PR in the same wave can claim `facade.rs` — it just rebases.
- Combining is sometimes the *better review*, not merely the cheaper one. Two halves of one
  security protocol (server exchange + browser key custody) reviewed separately means no review
  ever sees the binding between them.

Related: [[project-worktree-branch-ref-goes-stale]] when re-batching into an existing branch.

- **Cooled, no longer needs an ownership zone:** `gate/floor.rs` + `seams/floor_store.rs` (606/107

`rotation/reseal.rs` + `rotate.rs`.

changes ripple. The recurring failure is the semantic merge conflict in
[[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]] — two PRs both MERGEABLE that break main's compile

**How to apply:** batch so each PR *owns* its hot files exclusively, and sequence any PR carrying a
signature change ahead of everything touching its callers. Group small issues that collide on the
same interface into ONE PR rather than trying to parallelize them — this also conserves the
CodeRabbit quota (see [[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]]). Reserve worktree isolation
for the batches that genuinely run concurrently.

**Re-confirm the map after every merge wave.** Closing issues retires rows, but merges also *create*

a `gate/adoption.rs` issue but also edits `rotation/reseal.rs`, colliding with a different wave).

Dependency edges between issues must be recorded with **GitHub's native issue-dependency
feature**, not a prose `## Depends on` / `## Blocks` section in the body.

**Why:** prose edges are error-prone. They are hand-maintained in two places, so the reverse
edge silently rots — an audit on 2026-08-02 found forward edges present and well-written on 17
recently-filed issues while **zero of seven** upstreams reciprocated. The native feature writes
both directions from a single call and surfaces in the issue UI and list filters, so it cannot
drift.

**How to apply** (the API is live on FSM1/cipher-box):

```bash
# add: issue N is blocked by issue M — pass M's DATABASE id, not its number
ID=$(env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<M> --jq '.id')
env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api -X POST \
  repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=$ID

# read either direction
env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N>/dependencies/blocked_by
env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh api repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/<N>/dependencies/blocking
```

`issue_id` is the numeric `.id`, NOT the issue number — passing the number silently targets the
wrong issue. Posting `blocked_by` on N makes N appear under M's `blocking` automatically; never
write both sides by hand.

Keep prose only where it carries rationale the link cannot (why the dependency exists, what
specifically is inherited). Delete bare restatements of the edge itself.
